name: Cica / Centella asiatica

lead: Cica is skincare shorthand for Centella asiatica, or gotu kola, a herb used traditionally for skin conditions and minor wounds. Its extracts appear in soothing creams and serums.
Wikipedia notes that clinical efficacy and safety have not been proven in clinical research, and no study on pigment recovery was found.

paras: Its main active compounds are triterpenoids such as asiaticoside and madecassoside; the sources reviewed do not describe a pigment mechanism.
Topical use can cause contact dermatitis or irritation. Oral products have been linked in case reports to liver disease and may cause drowsiness.

lead: Cica is the common skincare shorthand for Centella asiatica, a perennial herb in the Apiaceae family also called gotu kola or Asiatic pennywort. Extracts and isolated triterpenoids are used in soothing creams and serums, including products marketed for skin recovery after blemishes.[1]

Its main constituents are pentacyclic triterpenoids and their glycosides, notably asiatic acid, madecassic acid and the derivatives asiaticoside and madecassoside. Wikipedia reports that the plant has traditional use for dermatological conditions and minor wounds, but that clinical efficacy and safety have not been proven in clinical research.[1]
The sources gathered for this entry do not include any clinical study of cica for post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.
infobox: Asiaticoside, madecassoside, asiatic acid, madecassic acid[1]
Topical (cosmetic); also eaten as a leafy green[1]

paras: The plant is native to tropical regions of Africa, Asia, Australia and western Pacific islands and grows in swampy areas. About 124 compounds have been identified from it, chiefly triterpenoids and their glycosides.[1]
It has been used in traditional medicine for various disorders, skin conditions and minor wounds, and is eaten as a leafy green in several Asian cuisines.[1]

No studies found of Centella asiatica for post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation or appearance outcomes in the sources reviewed. Wikipedia states that clinical efficacy and safety of the plant have not been proven in clinical research.[1]

Topical use can cause contact dermatitis and irritation, and eating it may cause drowsiness. Reviews published in 2024 linked foods and supplements containing the plant to jaundice and liver disease, with case reports of liver disease after several weeks of use.[1]
